title: Eira and the Troll's Cookie
markdown:
High up in the rocky steep peaks where the air tasted like clean snow and sunshine, lived an elf named Eira. She was not the sort of elf you read about in faraway castles. Eira was mountain-bred, strong and sturdy, with eyes the colour of moss at twilight and hands that knew their way around a climbing rope as well as a delicate wildflower. Her dearest companion was Lentil, a snow hare whose fur was the purest white. He blended in with the high-country drifts so well you would only spot him by the twitch of his long sensitive ears. Lentil was more than a pet. He was Eira’s shadow, her alarm clock, and sometimes her very best thought-sparker. He had a nose that could sniff out a particularly juicy mountain berry from a mile away, and ears that could hear a whispered secret on the wind.

Eira needed a sprig of Moonpetal. It was a herb that only bloomed near the Whispering Falls, a place a good climb away. It was for her grandmother, who had a cough that sounded like pebbles rattling in a tin. Gran’s lullabies were usually sung in a strong clear voice. Lately little scratchy noises punctuated the songs.

“Come on, Lentil,” Eira said, tying her sturdy boots. The leather was worn smooth from many journeys. “We’ve a bit of a trek ahead. The Moonpetal won’t pick itself, and Gran needs it before sundown.” Lentil gave a happy thump of his hind leg, little snow-white tail bobbing. He was always ready for an adventure, especially if it involved exploring new smells and possibly a stray delicious-smelling crumb.

The path wound upwards through fir trees that whispered secrets to the wind. Their needles, sharp and green, tickled Eira’s nose as she passed. The air grew cooler, crisp and clean. The world below faded like a forgotten dream, becoming a patchwork of greens and browns far beneath them. And then, as they rounded a particularly sharp bend, where the rocks jutted out like the teeth of a slumbering giant, Eira saw it. Beneath a ruined tower, silhouetted against the pale sky, mist was moving through the dark fir trees like a shy grey serpent. It curled around the ancient stones of the tower, making it look even more mysterious. It was a grand sight, even if it was a little bit spooky. Lentil’s ears flattened slightly against his head, but he stayed right by Eira’s side, a brave little puff of white fur against the imposing landscape.

Soon they came to a narrow pass, so tight you could barely stretch your arms. It felt as if the mountain itself was squeezing them gently forward. And right in the middle of it, blocking their way, was a bridge. Not just any bridge, but a very old, very sturdy stone bridge spanning a chasm that looked deep enough to swallow a whole flock of sheep. And on the bridge stood a bridge keeper. This bridge keeper was not your average sort of chap. He was a troll, a rather portly one, with a beard like a tangled bramble patch and a nose that looked as if it had been squashed by a falling boulder and then never quite straightened out. He wore spectacles that were far too small for his face, perched dangerously on the very end of his nose. He clutched a very important-looking piece of parchment, as if it held the secrets of the universe.

“Halt,” boomed the troll, voice like stones grinding together in a quarry. “None shall pass the Bridge of Sighs without filling out Form 7B: The Declaration of Intent to Cross.”

Eira blinked. “Form 7B? But I just need to cross to get to the Whispering Falls. My grandmother is unwell, and she needs a special herb.”

“A form is a form, missy,” the troll grumbled, tapping the parchment with a thick finger that looked more like a sausage. “And this one requires your grandmother’s favourite colour, the third word of the song you sang yesterday, and the estimated wing-span of the smallest bird you’ve ever seen.” He adjusted his spectacles, which threatened to slide right off.

Eira’s brow furrowed. Her grandmother’s favourite colour? She had never asked. Gran loved the colour of the sky after a rain shower, but was that blue, or sky-blue, or perhaps hope-blue? And the third word of yesterday’s song? Eira remembered humming a little tune while she was mending a sock, but she had been humming without words. And the bird’s wingspan? This was altogether too much fuss for such a simple journey. Lentil, sensing Eira’s frustration, gave a little squeak and nudged her hand with his nose. He did not like the troll’s stern face one bit; it made his own sensitive ears twitch nervously.

Eira looked at the troll’s official-looking parchment, then at the impossibly deep chasm. “Perhaps there’s another way around. Or perhaps someone who understands these forms better could help us. Someone who knows what the troll truly means.” She looked at Lentil, who twitched his nose towards a faint sweet smell wafting from a small cave just off the path, not far from the bridge. The smell was warm and inviting, like a hug on a cold day.

“That way smells delicious,” Lentil squeaked, a tiny whisper that only Eira could hear. He was already imagining what sort of delights might be found there.

“You’re right, Lentil,” Eira replied, a spark of an idea igniting. “Let’s investigate.” Following the delicious aroma led them to the very mouth of a cave, where a most unusual sight awaited them. Inside, amidst bags of flour and sacks of sugar that rose like little snowy hills, was an ogre. But this was no ferocious cave-dwelling brute, the kind you might hide from under your bed. This was Grok, the Ogre Baker. His apron was dusted with flour, giving him a cheerful cloud-like appearance. His hands, though enormous, were surprisingly gentle as he kneaded a giant ball of dough. The cave smelled wonderfully of cinnamon and warm bread, a scent that made Eira’s stomach rumble appreciatively.

“Well, hello there,” rumbled Grok, voice a deep rumbling sound like distant thunder, but friendly and warm. “Lost, are we? Come in, come in. Just mind the rising dough; it’s very important work.” He gestured with a flour-dusted hand towards a clear spot on the cave floor.

Eira explained their predicament, the strange Form 7B, and the stubborn troll. Grok listened patiently, large kind eyes blinking slowly like a wise old owl. He stopped his kneading for a moment, wiping his brow with the back of his hand. “Ah, the Bridge Keeper’s forms,” he sighed, voice soft. “He means well, that troll. He’s very concerned with rules and order. But he’s forgotten how to make things simple. He’s been making little puzzles, hoping people will show him they’re clever enough to get past. And the answers he wants aren’t really answers at all; they’re just things that prove you can think a little, that you can look at things from a different angle.”

Grok chuckled, a sound like a happy boulder rolling downhill. “I cannot give you the answers, for that would be cheating. But I can give you something that might just help. What if I made you a little something? Something that looks official, but is just a good distraction. Something that proves you’ve thought about things, in a tasty sort of way.”

And with surprising speed, Grok began to work. He mixed a special dough, one that rose high and smelled heavenly, a blend of sunshine and sweetness. He rolled it out thin, like a magic carpet, and then, with his big fingers, he carefully pressed patterns into it. He made it into a round shape, like a very official looking biscuit. Then he wrote in edible ink, made from the juice of plump mountain berries, a few very official-looking symbols.

“There,” he said, presenting Eira with a beautifully decorated, rather large cookie. It was almost as big as Lentil. “This is my Declaration of Delicious Intent. It’s got a picture of a mountain, for your home, a little hare for your friend, and a swirl for the wind. It looks very important, doesn’t it? And it smells quite delightful, if I do say so myself.”

Eira looked at the cookie, marvelling at its artistry. Lentil, who had been watching with wide curious eyes, sniffed it with great interest. He gave a little hop of approval. “It’s perfect, Grok. Thank you.” Eira carefully took the cookie, wrapping it in a soft cloth.

Armed with Grok’s creation, Eira and Lentil returned to the bridge. The troll was still there, looking bored, spectacles threatening to slide off completely. He was tapping his foot impatiently.

“Ah, back again?” he grumbled, though without his earlier gruffness. “Have you filled out Form 7B?”

Eira stepped forward, holding out the cookie with great ceremony. She felt a little thrill of excitement, a mix of nerves and pure ingenuity. “Indeed I have,” she said, voice clear and steady. “Here is my Declaration of Intent to Cross. It details my desire to reach the Whispering Falls for a specific purpose, and it demonstrates my understanding of the importance of clear communication and thoughtful presentation.” She pointed to the edible ink. “As you can see, the symbols represent my home, my companion, and the very air we breathe. It’s quite comprehensive, wouldn’t you agree?”

The troll squinted at the cookie, small eyes widening. He leaned closer, brow furrowed in concentration. He poked it. It smelled wonderful, a scent that reminded him of his own mother’s baking, long ago. He had never seen anything like it. It looked official, yet utterly delightful. He was so surprised by the sheer cleverness of it, and so taken by the delicious smell, that for the first time all day he actually smiled. It was a surprising crinkly smile that made him look less like a boulder and more like a friendly rock formation.

“Well, I’ll be,” he muttered, voice losing some of its gravelly tone. “That’s very good. Very demonstrative. You’ve really thought about it.” He waved a hand, the parchment forgotten for a moment. “Go on, then. Pass.”

Eira and Lentil hurried across the bridge, Eira giving Lentil a knowing wink. They soon reached the Whispering Falls, and there, glowing softly in the spray that kissed the air, was the Moonpetal. Its petals were a pale silvery white, like captured moonlight. Eira carefully gathered a few sprigs, heart light, mission accomplished. She looked at Lentil, who was happily nibbling on a tiny crumb of Grok’s cookie that had fallen.

“We did it, Lentil,” she whispered. “And we didn’t even need to know Grandmother’s favourite colour. Or the exact wing-span of the smallest bird.”

As they made their way home, the mist still drifted through the fir trees, but it seemed less spooky now, more like a gentle blanket settling over the mountains. Gran would have her herb before sundown. The troll still had his forms. And somewhere in a floury cave, Grok was already kneading the next day’s dough, as if official biscuits were simply another kind of bread.
characters: Eira (a mountain-bred elf), Lentil (a pure-white snow hare), Grok (a flour-dusted ogre baker)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
